七、生前所取之物，皆藏影中。影中之物，可取。

（写至此处，字迹陡然加重。）
我照着做了。
我都照着做了。
我还是出不去——

为何，为何，为何，为何，为何。

为何，为何，为何，为何，为何。

（旁侧另有一行新墨）
八、阴市无五供。
有
无
有
无
（最后一处，有、无二字叠在一起，辨不清先后。）
en:
Old Unsigned Note

Remember. Follow these exactly:
I. At the stalls of the Nether Market, you may look, but never take.
II. To obtain the candle fire, first gather the Five Offerings.
III. The Five Offerings are: White Mouth, Green Strands, Black Path, Yellow Dusk, and Red Joy.
IV. The Nether Market has the White Mouth.
V. The Nether Market has the Red Joy.
VI. When the Five Offerings are gathered, the candle fire shall reveal itself.
VII. All that was taken in life lies hidden in the shadows. What lies in the shadows may be taken.

(Here the strokes turn suddenly heavy.)
I did exactly as it said.
I followed every step.
And still I cannot get out.

Why. Why. Why. Why. Why.

Why. Why. Why. Why. Why.

(A line of fresher ink runs down the side.)
VII. The Nether Market does not have the Five Offerings.
It does
It does not
It does
It does not
(At the very end, "does" and "does not" are written one atop the other, and there is no telling which came first.)

所以美美从来不跟普通的猫玩。可这片儿的猫就这么多，拒绝着拒绝着，再会社交的小猫咪，也不想再来找美美了。

美美今夜特意没有睡觉。它听到窝外边有了响动，嗷地一声窜出去，正扑倒了一只黑白相间的猫。
这只黑白相间的猫吓了一大跳，布满毛的脸上出现了可疑的红晕，跑得可快可快。
美美在原地舔了舔爪子。淑女是不会追去的，就等它下次再来吧。
en:
Beauty is, without a doubt, the most beautiful cat around.
With her calico coat and the little flower she always wears behind her ear, she is a vision.
So, of course, she doesn't play with the common cats. One by one, they stop trying.
But then, strange gifts begin appearing at her nest. A perfect, shiny scale. A pretty, dried fish. And each one is dusted with black and white fur.
One night, Beauty stays awake. Hearing a rustle, she pounces and lands on a startled tuxedo cat.
The cat's furry face flushes bright red, and it shoots away into the night.
Beauty just licks her paw, unfazed. A lady never chases.
He'd be back.

《论丧葬》
士人资财千万，父母丧故，仪礼周备，丧三年，一掷万贯以彰其爱。
贫民流徙，衣不蔽体，食不果腹，土地棺椁，倾命亦不可得。取所睡茅席，裹尸一炬，停丧三日而已。
两相较之，于是谓士人知礼而民不肖。
无资财者，无爱父母亲友之格乎？此即孔某之礼耶？岂真不知万贯之财，于大富之家不过鸿毛。茅席一张，停丧三日，于贫民之家，几近死矣！
丧葬儒礼，事死繁及至碍生，谬甚！
en:
On Funeral Rites
Rich families spend fortunes on elaborate funerals and three years of mourning to show filial piety. Poor families, struggling just to survive, can't afford a burial plot or coffin. They wrap their dead in straw and burn them, mourning just three days.
People say the rich know proper respect, while the poor lack filial love. But does having no money mean you don't love your parents? Is this the "propriety" that man Kong preaches? Does he truly not realize that ten thousand strings of cash are but a feather to the wealthy and that a straw mat and brief mourning are everything to the poor? Confucian funeral customs are so complex that they burden the living more than honor the dead. An utter absurdity!

zh:
诸位山民、同道：
探探奇案，解解心忧。
不知大家有没有发现，山中的怪声已经消失多日。
有人问是不是阿枫出手了，这里统一回复一下——嘿嘿，解决问题的不是阿枫，但事件真相已水落石出！那怪声因合乐社重建而起，也因#Y$N#E出手相助而终。
几日前，阿枫和解忧司同僚也去听了合乐社的初次排练。没想到真是如听仙乐耳暂明啊，阿枫采访到了合乐社社员余歌师姐，让我们听听她怎么说——
余歌：……没想到会惊扰到山中诸位的生活，真是抱歉。那些怪声是由我祖父的留声匣机巧传出，并非装神弄鬼。今后我们会在专门的地方排练，哦对了，我们的社长是精通音律、心地善良的#Y$N#E，欢迎大家加入我们一起寻找歌唱的乐趣！
……
总而言之，这桩奇案到此也告一段落了，解忧司在这里也祝贺合乐社重振旗鼓，越办越好！
en:
Dear Mountain Dwellers and Fellow Disciples,
A strange mystery solved, and one less thing to worry about.
Have you noticed? The strange noises in the mountains have been gone for days now.
Some have asked whether I was the one who solved it. So let's clear that up: not quite. The mysterious sounds were caused by the renovation of the Harmony Troupe, and with help from #Y$N#E, they've finally come to an end.
.
A few days ago, my colleagues and I visited the Harmony Troupe's first rehearsal. So beautiful it cleared the mind. I interviewed Senior Sister Yu Ge of the troupe. Here's what she had to say:
Yu Ge: "...We never meant to disturb the peace of the mountain. Our humblest apologies. Those strange noises came from my grandfather's Voice Box. They weren't meant to scare anyone. From now on, we'll rehearse in a proper designated place. Oh, and our club president is #Y$N#E, who's both musically gifted and incredibly kind. We'd love for everyone to join us and share in the joy of singing."
...
In short, this little mystery is now wrapped up. The Bureau of Relief is happy to see the Harmony Troupe back on its feet, and we wish them all the best going forward!

夜聚昼散，鬼市子的灯笼升起又落下好多好多轮。当初莽莽撞撞闯进这里的大侠却好久没回。
小禄想，大侠是不是去江湖了？江湖好玩吗？江湖在哪里呀？
小褔大喊：“那我们就去问问嘛！”
三人跑进鬼市子，问牛头，牛头说，江湖嘛，就是刀啊剑啊的一通乱打。
小禄摇摇头，这真没意思。
她们问银婆婆，银婆婆说，这里就是啊。
小寿摇摇头，这里？鬼市子算是江湖吗？
道主们到茶馆里听说书。鬼先生又在讲与契丹的大战，讲朱帮主，讲鬼市子的阴兵。
道主们点点头，哦，对了，这我们知道的，这真是江湖呢！可是先生，江湖人不是都来来去去找不见的，阴兵怎么一直在这里？
鬼先生道：“大抵是心愿未偿。”
“什么心愿？”
先生道：“或是未曾得见——
⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛”
en:
As night fell, the lanterns of the Ghostlight Market rose again, as they had through countless turnings of day and night. Yet the wanderer who once recklessly stumbled into this place has not returned for a long, long time.
Lu wondered if the hero had gone off into the jianghu. Was the jianghu a fun place? And where exactly was it?
"Then let's go ask!" Fu cried out.
The three ran into the Ghostlight Market and asked Niu Tou. Niu Tou replied, "The jianghu? It's just a chaotic brawl of clashing sabers and swords."
Lu shook her head. That didn't sound like any fun at all.
Then they asked Granny Yin. Granny Yin said, "Why, this place right here is the jianghu."
Shou shook her head. "Here? Does the Ghostlight Market count as the jianghu?"
The Dao Lords went to the teahouse to listen to storytelling. Mr. Ghost was there again, telling of the great war with the Khitan, of Chief Zhu, and of the spectral soldiers of the Ghostlight Market.
The Dao Lords nodded. "Oh, right, we know that part. This really is the jianghu! But sir, aren't people of the jianghu always coming and going without a trace? Why have the spectral soldiers stayed here all this time?"
Mr. Ghost said, "Most likely, their final wishes remain unfulfilled."
"What wishes?"
Mr. Ghost replied, "Perhaps they never lived to see..."

en: Niu Ben often feels helpless in the face of his father's stubbornness, but no matter how hard he tries, he can never change the old man's mind. Back in the Forsaken Quarter, his father, Niu Mang, had taken to the streets to sell steamed veggies with flour after witnessing how many neighbors were struggling to afford even a single meal. The price he charged was next to nothing, and whenever children came by, he would ladle in extra sesame oil and toss in wild mushrooms and meat broth. It was a business that brought no profit, but Niu Mang never uttered a word of complaint. He simply wanted to ease the hardship of those around him in whatever small way he could. After the Unbound Cavern took control of the District, the area became a haven for swordsmen, and some of them, too, began lining up at Niu Mang's stall. Noticing this, he quietly added a new dish stir-fried chicken noodles, priced a little higher, onto his menu. Niu Ben observes it all in silence. He doesn't interfere but supports his father, secretly paying the Unbound Cavern a protection fee, just to make sure no one will lay a hand on the old man or his humble little stall.

Water from other ditches flowing into great waters and the sea is Chuan Water. Water issuing from the earth but not flowing is Yuan Water. These five waters may be used for benefit or dammed, but they are not constant, and danger lies therein.

……
胡子又言“天降甘露”，命大赦，而狱中实增囚百余人。上下以欺罔为常。

右件皆弟子亲勘，谨录以闻。续有风动，嗣当驰报。
en:
Xingwang Prefecture Secret Report Summary
...
The Emperor Chang indulges in banquets and hands all state affairs over to the witch, Fan Huzi. Dressed in Taoist robes, Fan Huzi enters and exits the palace freely, making decisions in the name of the Jade Emperor's decree. Gong Chengshu and Lu Qiongxian both secured their power by flattering Fan Huzi. Official appointments are often made only after Fan Huzi signs them. Official selection departments secretly sell positions with fixed prices.
All trading in the city uses lead coins. Copper coins are banned in the city. The people only receive lead coins for their goods, but the government only accepts copper coins for taxes, fines, and grain payments. People with copper coins either melt them into utensils or bury them, so copper coins have disappeared from the market.
...
Fan Huzi also claimed "Sweet dew falling from heaven" and ordered a massive amnesty, but over a hundred prisoners were actually added to the jails. Deception is common from top to bottom.

Your disciple has personally verified these truths and recorded them for your eyes. Any further developments will be reported immediately.

zh: 惜此学本为学术之事，一与好名好利之人生干戈，便有许多波澜。旧器本在尘土之间，贵贱未分，一经考订，则知某为商周，某为秦汉，某为名贤旧藏，价遂十倍百倍。于是豪家巨室，争相购求，几有石崇、王恺斗富之风。石崇以劫客致富，已为后世所鄙，今人若因一器一铭，遂驱人发北邙之冢，则其罪恐甚于斗富矣。
en: It is a profound tragedy that a discipline born of pure scholarly devotion should breed such endless trouble the moment it crosses paths with worldly greed. While slumbering in the dust, antiquities carry no price; they are equal in their silence. Yet, the moment a relic is authenticated, traced back to the foundries of the Shang or Zhou dynasties, or proven to have graced the study of a historical luminary, its value swells a hundredfold. The wealthy and powerful rush to hoard them, sparking vulgar contests of extravagance reminiscent of the infamous rivalries of ancient lords. The ancient tyrant Shi Chong built his fortune on the blood of robbed merchants and earned the eternal scorn of history. But if today's collectors drive men to tear open the sacred, ancient tombs of Mount Beimang for the sake of a single bronze vessel or carved inscription, their sins are surely far darker than mere vanity.

zh:
早就听闻，这崇元殿是皇家的脸面。登基大典、大朝会、年尾大傩……凡是热闹的大事都在这里头举办。
我惦记了许久，今日总算蹭到了墙根底下！
但这守卫也，太！森！严！了！侧门压根进不得，要进大殿只得走正门，还得过层层盘查。还有那广场上，整整齐齐站满了禁军，听说是在为大典排演。那阵仗，看着都腿软。
不过，难不倒我——上边这些见闻，都是我趁着卫兵交班的空档，扒着墙头，一眼一眼偷扫见的。
眼下进不去，但我有个好主意：等大典那日再来查探！到时鼓乐震天、人来人往，指不定我就能跟着哪支捧花捧灯的队伍混进去！那时就算被抓……至少也亲眼瞧过了这满殿的繁华热闹，不亏！
en:
I've heard about Chongyuan Hall for ages. Coronations, grand court assemblies, year-end rites, if it's big enough, it happens there. I've been itching to see it for myself. Today I finally made it as far as the wall, but the security is insane.
Side gate is a dead end. Want the main hall, you have to go in from the front, and it's checkpoint after checkpoint. The square is packed with Imperial Guards in perfect ranks. They're rehearsing for the ceremony, that's what people say. Just looking at them makes my knees go weak. Still, when the guard shifts rotated, I managed to steal a few glimpses, peeking over the wall again and again.
No way I'm getting in today, but I've got a plan. On the day of the ceremony, with drums, crowds, and teams coming and going, I might be able to blend in. If I get caught... well. At least I'll have seen what it's like inside. Worth it.

Petition from the Monks of Liangzhou's Temples for General □□□

Since the Guiyi Army's triumphant march westward restored the Hexi lands to Tang rule, we monks have once again been blessed to honor the Buddha statues and revive the sacred Dharma tradition.
In times of famine, General □□□ opened the granaries to feed the hungry; when the fields lay barren, he personally led the effort to divert water from the garrison canal, bringing life-giving irrigation so the people could till the soil once more.
He commissioned the carving of grottoes to safeguard scriptures and precious texts, preserving the teachings of the Buddha for future generations. Moreover, he established schools far and wide, awakening the minds of countless children.
Now that the General's noble spirit has departed, the people grieve with broken hearts. On behalf of all, we humbly beseech:
First, that a solemn open Dharma assembly be held to transfer merit and guide the General's soul to peace.
Second, that a memorial altar be established, where offerings of incense may burn eternally in his honor.
Third, that the General's great deeds be inscribed within the sacred scripture caves, so that his legacy may stand side by side with the Dharma, revered by all generations to come.
(The name is smeared beyond recognition; beneath it, someone has scrawled in haste: "Not approved.")

zh:
大将军回来了！
村子燃起熊熊篝火，我依约将一碗清澈的水献到他面前。他仔细端详我的眉眼，爽朗地笑起来，抬手重重拍上我的肩头。没想到练武之人的力气如此之大，我一个不慎，手上的水碗猛地翻了跟头，重重地摔在地上——
咦？
睁开眼，面前是井下长长的坑道，被折断的工具七歪八扭着嘲笑我白日做梦。
是了。想走的人气势汹汹地找我大吵一架，带了好多人折断了镐子，丢下了铲子，便扬长而去。
爹用来记录的那本册子寻不着了。我另寻一本册子，像爹一样开始写记录。就着油灯的光，我几次拿起笔来，什么都没写，又放了下去。
他们不信我，也不信大将军了么？
不……不是这样的，只要循着图，一定能挖到的。
en:
The great general is back! 
The village lit a roaring bonfire, and I offered a bowl of clear water to him as promised. He stared intently at my face, laughed heartily, and raised his hand to pat me heavily on the shoulder. I never expected a martial artist to be so strong. I lost my balance, and the water bowl in my hand flipped over and crashed heavily to the ground... 
Hmm? 
When I opened my eyes, I was in the long underground tunnel. Broken tools lay askew, mocking my daydream. 
Right. Those who wanted to leave came to argue with me angrily, brought many people to break the pickaxes, threw down the shovels, and stormed off. 
The notebook my father used for records is gone. I found another notebook and started writing like he did. By the light of the oil lamp, I picked up the brush several times, but wrote nothing and put it down again. 
Do they not believe me, nor the great general anymore? 
No... That's not it. As long as we follow the map, we will surely find water.

en:
[Thrill] Great pay, steady post! Silver Needle is now the top pick for aspiring healers as the medical boom sweeps the land.
Good doctors never lack for work wherever they go. With the launch of the Healer's Reform, Silver Needle introduced the principle of "one life, one price" and offered top-tier compensation for physicians. As healers gained newfound respect, the healing arts surged in popularity. Silver Needle has since become one of the most sought-after sects for fledgling adventurers.

[Shock] After just two acne treatments at Silver Needle, the richest master is nearly bankrupt! 
As the weather turns chilly, the wealthy Master Wang finds himself teetering on the brink of ruin. Rumor has it that Master Li publicly mocked him for his acne, prompting Wang incensed to seek treatment at Silver Needle. There, his face was cleared, and so was his fortune. Still, Master Wang was pleased with the results, declaring that beauty comes at a price. Now blemish-free, he plans to make his debut at Revelry Hall and rebuild his fortune with charm alone.

暑风微变候，昼刻渐加数。

【晚】

en:
【Day and Night】

【Dawn】

Early Rising
Du Fu
In spring I often rise early,
For quiet things hold my heart.
I shore up stones to guard the bank,
Clear woods to reveal distant hills.
A single mound hides winding paths,
Leisurely steps lead me upward.
My servant returns from town,
A bottle of wine in hand.

Waking at Dawn
Bai Juyi
I turn my pillow, settle back to sleep,
Look back and give a lazy stretch.
The paper window brightens, I know it's dawn,
The cotton quilt warm, I feel spring's touch.
Don't force this idle nature of mine,
I must accept this aging frame.
With the rooster's crow, I sleep once more,
Not trading it for early court's claim.

【Day】

A Summer Day's Nap
Liu Zongyuan
Southern heat, damp and heavy as wine,
Leaning on the desk, I sleep by the north window fine.
At noon, alone, no other sound,
A mountain boy taps the tea mortar beyond the bamboo line.

Daytime Nap
Bai Juyi
Sitting straight in my white robe,
Rising to don straw sandals yellow.
After morning meal and washing done,
Slowly down the steps I go.
The summer breeze hints at change,
The daylight hours slowly grow.
The courtyard quiet, shaded deep,
Birds sing in trees with leaves new.
Walking alone, lying alone,
The summer scene is far from through.
If I don't nap at midday,
How can the long day be endured true?

【Dusk】

Mooring at Jiande River
Meng Haoran
My boat moors by misty isle,
Dusk deepens the traveler's woe.
Wilds vast, sky bows to trees,
River clear, the moon draws near.

On the Plain of Tombs
Li Shangyin
As dusk falls, my heart uneasy,
I drive my carriage up the ancient plain.
The setting sun is boundless in its beauty,
Yet twilight's hour is nigh again.

【Night】

Sitting Alone on an Autumn Night
Wang Wei
Sitting alone, I grieve my graying hair,
In empty hall, the second watch draws near.
Rain falls, mountain fruits drop,
Lamp light, grass insects sing clear.
White hair, in the end, cannot be changed,
Gold elixir, impossible to attain.
To know how to dispel old age and sickness,
Only by learning the way of no-birth's gain.

Village Night
Bai Juyi
Frosted grass, vast and gray, insects chirp faint,
North and south of the village, no traveler in sight.
Alone I step out the front gate, gaze at the fields,
Under bright moon, buckwheat flowers gleam like snow white.

zh: 唐同光四年，庄宗皇帝令轮番藩兵停驻清河，不得归镇，激起哗变。叛军横行，纵乱乡里。一少年欲离清河，众人劝之：“此间多乱，待定而后行。”少年云：“吾擅弓矢，贼来必殪，不足患。”行十里，入夜，道旁草中似有人声。少年呼之不应，连发数矢，人声依旧。少年惊，奔至树下，背负树而持弓矢对之。倏忽风雷突至，电光逐来，面前有物纷纷坠地。少年视之，乃树枝叶。少年恐惧，丢弓矢，仰空乞命，随即电光渐灭，风雷亦息。还顾大树，枝干尽矣。俄而一老叟现身，手持数矢，少年视之甚异，再拜之。老叟笑曰：“尔弓矢甚善，然亦需知剑术，方能无患。”少年请教名号，老叟云：“吾无名，剑亦无名。”请教剑术，老叟施剑技二三，风雷电光又至。终习得一技，竟成善剑者也。
en: In the fourth Year of the Tongguang Era, Emperor Zhuangzong's decree barring garrison troops from returning home sparked rebellion in Qinghe. As mutineers ravaged the countryside, a youth prepared to depart despite warnings: "The roads are chaotic. Wait until order is restored." He boasted, "I excel with bow and arrow. Should bandits come, I'll strike them down." Ten li into his journey, at nightfall, rustling sounds emerged from the roadside grass. The youth shouted but received no reply. He shot several arrows, yet the sounds persisted. Terrified, he retreated to a tree, pressing his back against it while nocking another arrow. Suddenly, wind and thunder erupted. Lightning flashed, and objects rained down before him, revealed as branches and leaves. The youth, trembling, cast aside his bow and begged for mercy. The storm ceased. Turning, he saw the tree stripped bare. An old man materialized, holding the fired arrows. The youth, astonished, bowed deeply. The old man laughed: "Your archery is fine, but without swordsmanship, you remain vulnerable." When asked his name, the elder replied: "I have none, nor does my sword." When the youth pleaded to learn his art, the old man demonstrated two or three techniques, with wind and lightning surging anew. Mastering but one move, the youth became a swordsman of renown.

黑豆五斗大麻子一斗五升青州枣一斗。黑豆净水淘过，蒸一遍，曝干，去皮，又蒸一遍，又曝令干。麻子以水浸去皮，共枣同入甑中，蒸熟取出，去枣核。三味一处烂捣，又再蒸一遍，团为拳大，又再蒸之。从初夜至夜半，令香熟，便去火，以物密盖之，经宿，曝干，捣罗为末，任性吃，以饱为度。若人依法服之，故得神仙。若是奇人服，即得长生。
en:
Grain-Fasting Method of the Old Mother of Mount Li
Take five dou of black beans, one dou and five sheng of hemp seeds, and one dou of Qingzhou jujubes. Rinse the black beans in clean water, steam them once, dry them in the sun, remove the skins, then steam and dry them again. Soak the hemp seeds in water and remove their husks, then steam them together with the jujubes. Once done, remove the jujube pits.
Mash the three ingredients together until soft, steam the mixture again, and form it into balls the size of a fist. Steam them once more, from dusk to midnight, until fragrant and fully cooked. Then remove them from the heat, cover them tightly, leave them overnight, dry them in the sun, and grind them into powder.
Eat as much as you like, enough to feel full. If taken according to the method, an ordinary person may attain transcendence; an exceptional one may achieve immortality.

zh:
鸦儿酿

她平生失约无数，然彼时闻燕北盟讯，知契丹飞龙余孽仍搜寻着不见山。
当即摒却万般俗务，出山截杀。
本欲助他一臂，孰料此去，竟被断一臂。
伤未愈时，她借短暂回山修养之际，曾试复造青儿酿。
奈何独臂力衰，只得一坛血酒……

又是一年，这日门前不知被谁放了一坛赤色果儿酿成的酒。
问应宁、应安，二人皆支吾不言。
此酒之味，迥异于青儿酿、猴儿酿。
清芬蕴藉，入喉柔顺，可惜酿者无言，饮者缄默。
所行之道不同，纵再好的酒，今也成了两般滋味。
en:
Raven Brew

She had broken countless promises in her life, but upon hearing that the remnants of the Khitan Flying Dragon were still searching for Hidden Mountain,
she immediately set aside all mundane affairs and left the mountain to intercept and kill.
She had intended to assist him, but unexpectedly, she lost an arm in the process.
While her wound was not yet healed, during a brief return to the mountain to recuperate, she tried to recreate Halcyon Brew.
But with only one arm, weak as she was, she could only produce a jar of blood wine...

Another year passed. One day, a jar of wine brewed from red fruits was placed at her door without anyone knowing who.
She asked Ying Ning and Ying An, but both mumbled evasively.
The taste of this wine was completely different from Halcyon Brew or Monkey Brew.
Subtle and smooth, gentle on the throat. It's a pity the brewer said nothing, and the drinker remained silent.
Though the paths they walked were different, even the finest wine now has two distinct flavors.

休沐日又到了，你那边可有甚好去处？我听说你又接了处产业，近来忙得脚不沾地，案头堆的文书怕是比岑夫子书房里的还高。
还记得小时候有一回，寒娘子考校你课业，问《礼记·月令》中“仲春之月，毋作大事，以妨农之事”何解。你不知道，急得到处乱看，最后眼珠子一转，搬出一套“人不休沐枉少年，休沐方可养生长寿身体棒”的道理来，说什么圣人都晓得按时休沐，何况凡人，所以你不解其意都是有出处的……最后被寒娘子罚抄三遍。
你非得拉上我躲在仓库里一起抄。我写得手酸，你倒好，写了两行便趴桌上睡了，口水淌了半张纸……最后还是我帮你抄完的。怎么如今长大了，反倒把当初教我的那套全忘了？
既是休沐，便该放下那些劳什子，去外头走走，看看草木生发。莫要再熬着了。从前师父教咱的养气拳，也记得打打，活动活动气血。
哦忘了说给你的休沐礼物，也附上了。
en:
It's my day off again. Anything fun to do on your end? I heard you just took on another business venture and have been so swamped you barely have time to breathe. The paperwork on your desk must be stacked higher than the books in Master Cen's study by now.
Remember when we were kids? Madam Han was quizzing you on your lessons and asked what a specific line from the Book of Rites meant. You had absolutely no clue. You started looking around frantically before finally spinning this whole philosophy out of thin air about how "a youth who doesn't rest is a youth wasted," and how taking breaks was the secret to a long, healthy life. You rambled on about how even the ancient sages knew when to take a vacation, so your lack of an answer was actually backed by the classics... Naturally, Madam Han made you copy the text three times as punishment.
You dragged me into the warehouse and got me to help you write lines. My hand was cramping up, and what were you doing? You wrote exactly two lines, fell asleep right there at the desk, and were drooling all over the paper. I ended up writing the whole thing for you! How is it that now you're all grown up, you've completely forgotten the very philosophy you preached back then?
Since it's a day off for everyone, put down all that tedious work. Take a walk outside and enjoy the spring air. Stop staying up so late working! And make sure you're still practicing the Vitality Fist our master taught us to keep your blood flowing.
Oh, almost forgot. I've attached a little gift for you. Enjoy!

zh:
冰轮宫的大师为少年起了新的名字，和其余师兄一样皆为月名——丹轮子。
月，正是世间吐纳修炼之人不可缺少的根基，也是冰轮宫众人的修习法门。
沉默的丹轮子乖顺服从，勤勉认真。白天他在丹房里刻苦钻研药理，夜晚则在团圃上看着明月出神。
在浩如烟海的经卷中，丹轮子发现了来自西边神奇土地的传说：以特殊的术法捞出月亮，便可得到稀绝的灵药。
灵药。丹轮子的手指颤抖着抚上这两个字。如果当初自己早一点，快一点，是不是就可以找到救回爷娘的药方？
丹轮子尝试所有学过的术法，在丹池、在河边、在清泉……但他始终捞不起水中的月亮。
师兄们笑他痴傻，而他只一遍一遍对着水中的月影掐诀，尝试捞起月亮。
最后，他辞别师父，再一次踏上了寻药的旅程。
en:
The master of the Ice Wheel Palace gave the boy a new name, like all his senior brothers—a name of the moon: Dan Lunzi, meaning "Crimson Wheel."
The moon is the essential foundation for all who practice cultivation in this world, and the core of the Ice Wheel Palace's teachings.
The silent Dan Lunzi was obedient, diligent, and earnest. By day, he studied pharmacology intently in the alchemy room; by night, he gazed at the bright moon from the courtyard, lost in thought.
Within the vast ocean of scriptures, Dan Lunzi discovered a legend from a mysterious western land: using a special art, one could scoop the moon from water and obtain a rare, potent medicine.
Medicine. Dan Lunzi's fingers trembled as they traced the characters. If he had been faster, earlier back then... could he have found the formula to save his parents?
Dan Lunzi tried every art he had learned—by the alchemy pool, by the river, at the clear spring... but he could never lift the moon from the water.
His senior brothers laughed at his foolishness. Yet he only repeated the gestures toward the moon's reflection, trying again and again to scoop it up.

zh:
【滕文公章句下】

陈代曰：不见诸侯，宜若小然。今一见之，大则以王，小则以霸。且志曰：枉尺而直寻，宜若可为也。
孟子曰：昔齐景公田，招虞人以旌，不至，将杀之。志士不忘在沟壑，勇士不忘丧其元。孔子奚取焉？取非其招不往也。如不待其招而往，何哉？且夫枉尺而直寻者，以利言也。如以利，则枉寻直尺而利，亦可为与？昔者赵简子使王良与嬖奚乘，终日而不获一禽。嬖奚反命曰：天下之贱工也。或以告王良，良曰：请复之。强而后可，一朝而获十禽。嬖奚反命曰：天下之良工也。简子曰：我使掌与女乘。谓王良，良不可，曰：吾为之范我驰驱，终日不获一；为之诡遇，一朝而获十。诗云：不失其驰，舍矢如破。我不贯与小人乘，请辞。御者且羞与射者比。比而得禽兽，虽若丘陵弗为也。如枉道而从彼，何也？且子过矣，枉己者，未有能直人者也。
景春曰：公孙衍、张仪岂不诚大丈夫哉！一怒而诸侯惧，安居而天下熄。
孟子曰：是焉得为大丈夫乎？子未学礼乎？丈夫之冠也，父命之；女子之嫁也，母命之。往送之门，戒之曰：往之女家，必敬必戒，无违夫子。以顺为正者，妾妇之道也。居天下之广居，立天下之正位，行天下之大道。得志，与民由之；不得志，独行其道。富贵不能淫，贫贱不能移，威武不能屈。此之谓大丈夫。
周霄问曰：古之君子仕乎？孟子曰：仕。
传曰：孔子三月无君，则皇皇如也，出疆必载质。公明仪曰：古之人三月无君则吊。三月无君则吊，不以急乎？
曰：士之失位也，犹诸侯之失国家也。礼曰：诸侯耕助，以供粢盛；夫人蚕缫，以为衣服。牺牲不成，粢盛不絜，衣服不备，不敢以祭。惟士无田，则亦不祭。牲杀、器皿、衣服不备，不敢以祭，则不敢以宴，亦不足吊乎？出疆必载质，何也？
曰：士之仕也，犹农夫之耕也。农夫岂为出疆舍其耒耜哉？
曰：晋国亦仕国也，未尝闻仕如此其急。仕如此其急也，君子之难仕，何也？
曰：丈夫生而愿为之有室，女子生而愿为之有家。父母之心，人皆有之，不待父母之命，媒妁之言，钻穴隙相窥，逾墙相从，则父母国人皆贱之。古之人未尝不欲仕也，又恶不由其道。不由其道而往者，与钻穴隙之类也。彭更问曰：后车数十乘，从者数百人，以传食于诸侯，不以泰乎？
孟子曰：非其道，则一箪食不可受于人；如其道，则舜受尧之天下，不以为泰。子以为泰乎？
曰：否。士无事而食，不可也。
曰：子不通功易事，以羡补不足，则农有余粟，女有余布。子如通之，则梓、匠、轮、舆皆得食于子。于此有人焉，入则孝，出则悌，守先王之道，以待后之学者，而不得食于子。子何尊梓、匠、轮、舆，而轻为仁义者哉？
曰：梓、匠、轮、舆，其志将以求食也。君子之为道也，其志亦将以求食与？
曰：子何以其志为哉？其有功于子，可食而食之矣。且子食志乎？食功乎？曰：食志。
曰：有人于此，毁瓦画墁，其志将以求食也，则子食之乎？曰：否。
曰：然则子非食志也，食功也。
万章问曰：宋，小国也，今将行王政，齐、楚恶而伐之，则如之何？
孟子曰：汤居亳，与葛为邻，葛伯放而不祀。汤使人问之曰：何为不祀？曰：无以供牺牲也。汤使遗之牛羊，葛伯食之，又不以祀。汤又使人问之曰：何为不祀？曰：无以供粢盛也。汤使亳众往为之耕，老弱馈食。葛伯率其民，要其有酒食黍稻者夺之，不授者杀之。有童子以黍肉饷，杀而夺之。书曰：葛伯仇饷。此之谓也。为其杀是童子而征之，四海之内皆曰：非富天下也，为匹夫匹妇复雠也。汤始征，自葛载，十一征而无敌于天下。东面而征，西夷怨；南面而征，北夷怨，曰：奚为后我？民之望之，若大旱之望雨也。归市者弗止，芸者不变。诛其君，吊其民，如时雨降，民大悦。书曰：徯我后，后来其无罚，有攸不惟臣，东征，绥厥士女，匪厥玄黄，绍我周王见休。惟臣附于大邑周。其君子实玄黄于匪以迎其君子，其小人箪食壶浆以迎其小人。救民于水火之中，取其残而已矣。大誓曰：我武惟扬，侵于之疆，则取于残，杀伐用张，于汤有光。不行王政云尔，苟行王政，四海之内皆举首而望之，欲以为君。齐，楚虽大，何畏焉？
……
en:
【Teng Wen Gong, Chapter II】

Chen Dai said, "Not meeting with the princes may seem like a small matter. But if you were to meet them once, the great result might be to make a king, and the small result might be to make a hegemon. Moreover, the Record says, 'By bending only one foot, you gain eight feet.' It seems to me that something might be done."
Mencius replied, "Formerly, the duke Jing of Qi, when hunting, summoned his gamekeeper with a flag. The gamekeeper would not come, and the duke was going to put him to death. A man of purpose never forgets that his end may be in a ditch or a stream; a brave man never forgets that he may lose his head. What was it that Confucius found in that gamekeeper to approve? He approved his not going to the summons, when it was not in the proper way. What should be thought of him, if he went before being summoned? Moreover, that saying about 'bending one foot to gain eight feet' is spoken with reference to the gain. If it is gain that is sought, then would it also be right to bend eight feet to gain one foot? Formerly, Zhao Jianzi sent Wang Liang to drive for his favorite Xi, but in the course of a whole day they did not get a single bird. The favorite Xi reported this, saying, 'He is the poorest driver in the world.' Someone told Wang Liang of this. Liang said, 'I beg leave to try again.' By dint of pressing, this was accorded to him, and in one morning they got ten birds. The favorite, reporting this, said, 'He is the best driver in the world.' Jianzi said, 'I will make him always drive for you.' When he told Wang Liang so, however, Liang refused, saying, 'I drove for him, strictly observing the proper rules for driving, and in the whole day he did not get one bird. I drove for him so as to deceive the birds, and in one morning he got ten. It is said in the Book of Poetry, "There is no failure in the management of their horses; the arrows are discharged like the blows of an axe." I am not accustomed to drive for a mean man. I beg leave to decline the office.' Thus this driver was ashamed to assist an archer. If, by assisting him, his pile of birds might be as high as a hill, he would not do it. If I were to bend my principles and follow those princes, of what kind would my conduct be? And you are wrong. Never has a man who has bent himself been able to make others straight."
Jing Chun said, "Are not Gongsun Yan and Zhang Yi really great men? Let them once be angry, and all the princes are afraid. Let them live quietly, and the flames of trouble are extinguished throughout the kingdom."
Mencius said, "How can such men be great men? Have you not studied the Book of Rites? At the capping of a young man, his father admonishes him. At the marrying away of a young woman, her mother admonishes her, accompanying her to the door on her leaving, and cautioning her with these words, 'You are going to your home. You must be respectful; you must be careful. Do not disobey your husband.' Thus, to look upon compliance as their correct course is the rule for women. To dwell in the wide house of the world, to stand in the correct seat of the world, and to walk in the great path of the world; when he obtains his desire for office, to practice his principles for the good of the people; and when that desire is disappointed, to practice them alone; to be above the power of riches and honors to make dissipated, of poverty and mean condition to make swerve from principle, and of power and force to make bend — these characteristics constitute the great man."
Zhou Xiao asked, saying, "Did superior men of old times take office?" Mencius replied, "They did."
The Record says, "If Confucius was three months without being employed by some ruler, he looked anxious and unhappy. When he passed from the boundary of a state, he was sure to carry with him his proper gift of introduction." Gongming Yi said, "Among the ancients, if an officer was three months unemployed by a ruler, he was condoled with."
Mencius said, "The loss of his place to an officer is like the loss of his kingdom to a prince. It is said in the Book of Rites, 'A prince ploughs himself, and is assisted by the people, to supply the millet for sacrifice. His wife keeps silkworms, and unwinds their cocoons, to make the garments for sacrifice.' If the victims be not perfect, the millet not pure, and the dress not complete, he does not presume to sacrifice. 'And the scholar who, out of office, has no holy field, in the same way, does not sacrifice.' For the victims, the vessels, and the garments not being complete, he does not presume to sacrifice, and then neither may he dare to feel at ease. Is there not here sufficient ground also for condolence?"
Zhou Xiao again asked, "What was the meaning of Confucius's always carrying his proper gift of introduction with him, when he passed over the boundaries of the state where he had been?" "An officer's being in office," was the reply, "is like the ploughing of a husbandman. Does a husbandman part with his plough, because he goes from one state to another?"
Zhou Xiao pursued, "The kingdom of Jin is one, as well as others, of official employment, but I have never heard of anyone being thus earnest about being in office. If there should be this earnest desire, why does a superior man make any difficulty about taking it?"
Mencius answered, "When a son is born, what is desired for him is that he may have a wife; when a daughter is born, what is desired for her is that she may have a husband. This feeling of the parents is possessed by all men. If the young people, without waiting for the orders of their parents, and the arrangements of the go-betweens, shall bore holes to steal a sight of each other, or get over the wall to be with each other, then their parents and all other people will despise them. The ancients did indeed always desire to be in office, but they also hated being so by any improper way. To go to get office by an improper way is of a class with boring holes."
Peng Geng asked, saying, "Is it not an extravagant procedure to go from one prince to another and live upon them, followed by several tens of carriages, and attended by several hundred men?" Mencius replied, "If there be not a proper ground for taking it, a single bamboo-cup of rice may not be received from a man. If there be such a proper ground, then Shun's receiving the kingdom from Yao is not to be considered excessive. Do you think it excessive?"
Peng Geng said, "No. But for a scholar performing no service to receive his support notwithstanding, is not proper."
Mencius answered, "If you do not have an intercommunication of the productions of labor, and an interchange of men's services, so that one from his overplus may supply the deficiency of another, then husbandmen will have a superfluity of grain, and women will have a superfluity of cloth. If you have such an interchange, carpenters and carriage-wrights may all get their food from you. Here now is a man, who, at home, is filial, and abroad, respectful to his elders; who watches over the principles of the ancient kings, awaiting the rise of future learners — and yet you will refuse to support him. How is it that you give honor to the carpenter and carriage-wright, and slight him who practises benevolence and righteousness?"
Peng Geng said, "The aim of the carpenter and carriage-wright is to seek for a living. Is it also the aim of the superior man in his practice of principles thereby to seek for a living?" "What have you to do," returned Mencius, "with his purpose? He is of service to you. He deserves to be supported, and should be supported. And let me ask — Do you remunerate a man's intention, or do you remunerate his service?" Peng Geng said, "I remunerate his intention."
Mencius said, "There is a man here, who breaks your tiles, and draws unsightly figures on your walls — his purpose may be thereby to seek for his living. But will you indeed remunerate him?" "No," said Peng Geng; and Mencius then concluded, "That being the case, it is not the purpose which you remunerate, but the work done."
Wan Zhang asked, saying, "Song is a small state. Its ruler is now setting about to practice true royal government, and Qi and Chu hate and attack him. What in this case is to be done?"
Mencius replied, "When Tang dwelt in Bo, he was adjacent to the state of Ge, the chief of which was living in a dissolute state and neglecting his proper sacrifices. Tang sent messengers to inquire why he did not sacrifice. He replied, 'I have no means of supplying the necessary victims.' On this, Tang caused oxen and sheep to be sent to him, but he ate them, and still continued not to sacrifice. Tang again sent messengers to ask him the same question as before, when he replied, 'I have no means of obtaining the necessary millet.' On this, Tang sent the mass of the people of Bo to go and till the ground for him, while the old and feeble carried their food to them. The chief of Ge led his people to intercept those who were thus charged with wine, cooked rice, millet, and paddy, and took their stores from them, while they killed those who refused to give them up. There was a boy who had some millet and flesh for the laborers, who was thus slain and robbed. What is said in the Book of History, 'The chief of Ge behaved as an enemy to the provision-carriers,' has reference to this. Because of his murder of this boy, Tang proceeded to punish him. All within the four seas said, 'It is not because he desires the riches of the kingdom, but to avenge a common man and woman.' When Tang began his work of executing justice, he commenced with Ge, and though he punished eleven states, he had not an enemy in the kingdom. When he pursued his work in the east, the rude tribes in the west murmured. So did those on the north, when he was engaged in the south. Their cry was — 'Why does he make us last?' Thus, the people's longing for him was like their longing for rain in a time of great drought. The frequenters of the markets stopped not. Those engaged in weeding in the fields made no change in their operations. While he punished their rulers, he consoled the people. His progress was like the falling of opportune rain, and the people were delighted. It is said in the Book of History, 'We have waited for our prince. When our prince comes, we may escape from the punishments under which we suffer.' 'There being some who would not become the subjects of Zhou, king Wu proceeded to punish them on the east. He gave tranquility to their people, who welcomed him with baskets full of their black and yellow silks, saying — "From henceforth we shall serve the sovereign of our dynasty of Zhou, that we may be made happy by him." So they joined themselves, as subjects, to the great city of Zhou.' Thus, the superior men of that time brought baskets full of black and yellow silks to meet the superior men of Zhou, and the lower classes brought baskets of rice and vessels of congee to meet the lower classes of Zhou. So the people of Zhou saved them from the midst of fire and water, seizing only their oppressors. It is said in the Great Declaration, 'My power shall be put forth, and, invading the territories of Ge, I will seize the oppressor. I will put him to death to punish him — so shall the greatness of my work appear, more glorious than that of Tang.' If the ruler of Song will practice true royal government, all within the four seas will lift up their heads, and look for his coming with desire. Though Qi and Chu were large and powerful, what would there be to fear from them?"

en:
With the Guiyi Army being sparse over the vast Hexi, a single misstep could let rebels slip into the city, bringing endless unrest. 
Following Tang precedent, tally tokens were made for merchants traveling between states. 

No one expected the day the general, having lost the very token he ordered made, would be barred from entering a city. 
The army craftsmen worked through the night, forging him an armguard tally to solve the crisis and prevent future loss. 

On his last night before departure, the general stood atop the market tower, gazing silently at the moonlight flowing over the armguard. 
Heading east, leaving home—this will have no use anymore.

The Nameless General disappeared with Shi Shouxin after he relinquished his command over the army.

散发乘夕凉，开轩卧闲敞。
荷风送香气，竹露滴清响。

en:
[Seasons I]

[Spring]

Nine Impromptu Quatrains I
Du Fu
The spring river's end makes me grieve, so free; I walk with staff where fragrant isles be.
The willow catkins dance in the wind with glee; the peach blossoms float where the waters flee.

Late Spring
Han Yu
The grass and trees know spring will soon depart; in myriad hues they vie for fragrance's art.
The willow and elm flowers have no grace; they only fly like snowflakes all through space.

Day by Day
Li Shangyin
Day after day spring light vies with sun's bright ray; on winding hill roads apricot blossoms scent the way.
When will my mind be free of all its care? To catch the floating threads a hundred feet in air.

[Summer]

Summer Day at the Southern Pavilion, Thinking of Xin the Elder
Meng Haoran
The mountain light fades to the west, the moon from east climbs up the sky.
With loosened hair I take the cool, my windows open, here I lie.
The lotus breeze sends scents around, the bamboo dew drops with a sigh.
I'd take my lute to play a tune, but who can hear and not deny?
Thus I recall my bosom friend, in midnight dreams I think and cry.

Summer in Heights
Li Bai
Too lazy to wave my white fan in the heat; naked I lie in the woods' green retreat.
My cap is hung on the rocky wall; my head bares to the pine breeze's fall.

Early Summer by the Pond
Bai Juyi
The spring pond fills at twilight glee, the summer trees in shade are free.
The boats like ferries drift with ease, the fences like a village please.
I touch the zither's mat with peace, the wine shop opens its release.
In idleness I have no deed, I play with my young grandchild's need.

A Quatrain on the Rear Pond of Qi'an Commandery
Du Mu
The chestnut leaves pierce duckweed in the emerald pool; summer orioles warble among the roses cool.
All day no one watches the drizzling rain; two mandarin ducks bathe their red feathers in twain.

zh:
破门村来了许多江湖人，王小手突然明白了为什么先生要走了。
他和爹娘说，爹娘只叫他别惹事。没了先生管教，没了同窗游戏，甚至隔壁和楼上的大爷都整日闭门不出。
王小手一个人坐在棋盘前，对着棋谱摆好了棋子。他正想左手同右手下棋，头顶却罩下了一层阴影。
“小孩，下棋呢？”
他发现往来的江湖人都还可以。起码他们不欺负小孩，也不烧杀抢掠，最多找他下棋，把他赢倒。
王小手时常会问一些江湖之事。有些人同他说，有些人不讲话。有人输了恼羞成怒踢了棋盘，就有人给他扶起来继续下。
“大侠，什么是江湖啊？”
王小手对面的人把帽檐压了压。
“你所在之处，就是江湖。”
王小手努努嘴角。
江湖人行走江湖之前，应当上过同一间私塾，叫什么“江湖人培训班”之类的。
要不怎么说话都一个样呢？
en:
When Brokegate Village was filled with swordsmen, he finally understood why the master had left.
He told his parents, but they only told him to stay out of trouble. With no master to scold him, no classmates to play with, even the old men from next door and upstairs kept their doors shut.
So Wang Xiaoshou sat alone, setting up the pieces just as the manuals showed. He was about to play left hand against right when a shadow fell across the board.
"Hey, kid. Playing?"
It turned out these wanderers were alright. At least they didn't bully kids or loot the village. Mostly, they just sat down to play him... and beat him soundly.
Wang Xiaoshou liked asking about the Jianghu. Some answered, some stayed silent. Some flipped the board in a fit after losing, then others quietly set it back up and kept playing.
"Great hero," he asked once, "where is the Jianghu?"
The man across from him tipped his hat lower.
"Where you stand is the Jianghu."
Wang Xiaoshou snorted.
Before these guys start walking the Jianghu, they must all go to the same school. Something like "Jianghu 101."
Otherwise, why do they all sound exactly the same?

zh:
长风万里，终度玉门。你来到了那座巍峨的城关之下。此刻，它已不是难以越过的雄关天堑，而是春风西行的驿站。在旌旗飘扬的风沙里，你仿佛又一次看到了那位白头将军，正站在城墙之上，远眺东方。他眼里所见，心中所念，口中所说的皆为一句话：长安，如今可好？你踌躇半晌，开口道……
#Y【长安很好。】你向将军讲述着繁华的长安，讲述着你在史书上读过的那些繁华，念着晚唐诗人们锦绣的诗句。长安，始终都好。#E
听闻你的回答，将军颔首沉吟，眼中似有热泪。“长安……是个很好，很好的地方。”将军浑厚苍凉的嗓音里带着怀念，也带着慨然。满城少年变白发，手中的锋镞依然，归唐之心依然。城中传来阵阵鼓声，似有千军万马列阵。你听不清他们口中呼喊的名字，但你知道，那是千万乡音汇成的两个字——长安。
en:
The endless winds travel thousands of miles, finally passing through Jade Gate Pass. You arrive beneath that towering fortress. It is no longer an impassable stronghold, but a waystation for the spring breeze journeying west. In the windblown sand, with banners snapping overhead, you seem to glimpse the white-haired general once more, standing atop the wall and gazing east. What he sees in his eyes, holds in his heart, and speaks on his lips all resolve into a single refrain: "How fares Chang'an now?" You hesitate for a long while and say...
#Y[Chang'an is well.] You tell the general of Chang'an in all its splendor, of the prosperity you read about in the histories, and of the jeweled verses penned by late Tang poets. Chang'an has always been well.#E
Hearing your answer, the general nods in silent thought, tears seemingly welling in his eyes. "Chang'an... is a very, very fine place." The general's deep and desolate voice carries a sense of nostalgia, as well as a profound sorrow. The youths of the city have turned white-haired, yet the weapons in their hands remain sharp, as does their resolve to return to the Tang. From within the city comes the rolling beat of drums, as if an army of thousands were falling into formation. You cannot clearly hear the name they cry, but you know it is a single name formed by thousands of homesick voices: Chang'an.

相传此地乃古之求仙处，昔有方士言：海外三山，仙人居之，怀不死药。
千年间，王侯将相皆争遣使，望空祷祝，入海祈药，然去者不返，返者无言。
岁久，野草侵径，断碣横卧，故事犹在耳中，行人之迹已绝于途。
某一日，冯道行至此处，立于杂草丛生之间，仰见云外微茫，良久而叹：“仙山在望”。相随弟子，面面相觑，莫解其意。冯道拊掌，决意架桥渡海。
众人涉怒涛，拨重云，果见山岳巍峨，赫然在眼。
en:
The immortal mountain stands within sight, a place where all radiance gathers.
It is told that this place was a site where men sought immortality. In ancient times, a Daoist declared: beyond the sea lie three mountains, where immortals dwell and hold within them the medicine of undying life.
For a thousand years, kings, lords, generals, and ministers all vied to send envoys, praying into the sky, sailing into the sea to beseech the medicine. Yet those who departed did not return, and those who returned spoke not a word.
As the years wore on, wild grass crept across the paths, and broken steles lay fallen on their sides. The old tales still lingered in the ear, yet the traces of passersby had long since vanished from the road.
One day, Feng Dao came walking to this place. He stood amid the overgrown weeds, gazed up at the faint and distant shapes beyond the clouds, and after a long while sighed: "The immortal mountain stands within sight." The disciples who accompanied him exchanged bewildered glances, none able to find the meaning of his words. Feng Dao clapped his hands, resolved then and there to build a bridge across the sea.
The company waded through raging waves and parted the heavy clouds. And there, sure enough, the mountains rose in towering majesty, sudden and unmistakable before their eyes.

While training at Silver Needle, Chen Zixi was especially fond of these fan techniques. Flashy and freewheeling in motion, they also lent him a certain swagger whenever he held a fan.
But he learned fast and grew bored just as quickly. Before long, he slipped back to Hangzhou under the pretense of "setting out as a healer." The Chen family elders brandished their walking sticks in fury, berated him for damaging relations between the two families, and cut off his allowance on the spot.
Chen Zixi was only too happy to be free. He left home with two jugs of good wine he had filched, fan in hand. Everyone at the hall let him go; they all knew that once the jugs ran dry, the boy would return begging for a fresh brew.

【玉藻第十三】

天子玉藻，十有二旒，前后邃延，龙卷以祭，玄端而朝日于东门之外，听朔于南门之外。闰月则阖门左扉，立于其中，皮弁，以日视朝，遂以食。日中而馂，奏而食。日少牢，朔月大牢。五饮：上水、浆、酒、醴、酏。卒食，玄端而居。动则左史书之，言则右史书之，御瞽几声之上下。年不顺成，则天子素服，乘素车，食无乐。
诸侯玄端以祭，裨冕以朝，皮弁以听朔于大庙。朝服以日视朝于内朝，朝，辨色始入。君日出而视之，退适路寝听政，使人视大夫，大夫退，然后适小寝，释服，又朝服以食，特牲，三俎，祭肺，夕深衣，祭牢肉，朔月少牢，五俎，四簋，子夘，稷食菜羹。夫人与君同庖。君无故不杀牛，大夫无故不杀羊，士无故不杀犬豕，君子远庖厨。凡有血气之类，弗身践也。至于八月不雨，君不举，年不顺成，君衣布搢本，关梁不租，山泽列而不赋，土功不兴，大夫不得造车马。
卜人定龟，史定墨，君定体。
君羔幦虎犆，大夫齐车，豹幦豹犆，朝车；士齐车，鹿幦豹犆。

en:
【Jade Tassels of the Emperor, Chapter Thirteen】

The Emperor wore a cap adorned with jade tassels, twelve in number, with pendants hanging before and behind, and a dragon-embroidered robe for sacrifices. In dark ceremonial robes, he greeted the sun outside the East Gate, and listened to the monthly announcements outside the South Gate. During an intercalary month, he would close the left leaf of the gate and stand within it, wearing a deerskin cap, and attend to court affairs by day, then proceed to dine. At midday, he would consume the remnants of the morning meal, with music playing during the meal. On ordinary days, he offered one sacrificial animal; at the new moon, he offered three. The five beverages were, in order of precedence: water, rice water, wine, sweet wine, and millet gruel. After finishing the meal, he would retire in dark ceremonial robes. When he acted, the Left Recorder chronicled it; when he spoke, the Right Recorder chronicled it. The blind musician-in-attendance would judge the pitch of sounds. If the year's harvest was not successful, the Emperor would wear plain white garments, ride in a plain carriage, and dine without music.
The feudal lords offered sacrifices in dark ceremonial robes, attended court in ceremonial robes of lower rank, and listened to the monthly announcements in the great temple wearing deerskin caps. They attended court in court robes during the day at the inner court; at dawn, they would enter only when colors could be distinguished. The lord would come out to see them at sunrise, then retire to the main hall to handle affairs of state, sending someone to check on the high officials. Only after the high officials had withdrawn would he retire to the smaller chamber, remove his court robes, and then don court robes again for dining. He would offer one animal, presented on three stands, and sacrifice the lungs. In the evening, he wore the deep robe and offered the meat of the sacrificial animal. At the new moon, he offered one animal, presented on five stands with four baskets of grain. On the days of Zi and Mao, he ate millet and vegetable soup. The lady shared the same kitchen as the lord. The lord did not slaughter an ox without reason, the high officials did not slaughter sheep without reason, and the officers did not slaughter dogs or pigs without reason. The gentleman kept himself far from the kitchen. For any creature with blood and breath, he would not personally harm it. If it did not rain by the eighth month, the lord would not hold grand feasts. If the year's harvest was not successful, the lord would wear cloth garments and insert a wooden pin in his cap, tolls at passes and bridges would be waived, mountains and marshes would be surveyed but not taxed, no earthworks would be undertaken, and high officials would not be allowed to build carriages or raise horses.
The diviner determined the tortoise shell, the recorder determined the ink marks, and the lord determined the interpretation of the omens.
For the lord's carriage, the cushion was of lambskin with tiger-striped edges; for the high officials' fasting carriage, the cushion was of leopard skin with leopard-striped edges, used as their court carriage; for the officers' fasting carriage, the cushion was of deerskin with leopard-striped edges.

zh:
迷驿舟，永远徘徊在沙漠中的无归之船。
悬泉驿始置汉武扬鞭之时，毁于西域战火连天之岁。 
最后的驿长坚守一生，纵音书断绝，亦不辍驿递之职。
幸哉，他终是穿越无垠瀚海，来到故国边境； 
哀哉，他被捉生流放，成为了千古奇冤的缚戎人。 
这一路的艰辛，这一生的流离，最后都化为满腔悲怆，半身荆棘。 
他再次返回无垠沙海，只为了寻得昔日同袍的身影。 
可最后留给他的，唯有寒风，胡杨，和那巍峨无言的孤城。 
驿长化为树船，徘徊在寒冷寂寥的永夜。 
树船迷失沙海，寻觅着猎猎飘扬的旌旗。
en:
Wandering Ark is an eternal wanderer lost in the heart of the desert, a vessel without a home.

Celestial Spring Station was founded during the reign of Emperor Wu of Han and destroyed when war consumed the Western Regions.

Its last postmaster held his post for life, maintaining his courier duties even after all communication ceased. He crossed the boundless sands and reached his homeland's frontier, only to be seized and exiled. He was mistaken for an enemy captive, an injustice that echoes through the ages.

The hardships of the road and a lifetime adrift hardened into grief and thorns. He returned to the endless desert seeking traces of his comrades, but found only bitter winds, poplars, and a lone fortress standing in silence.

The courier became an ark, wandering through the cold, desolate eternal night. Lost in the sea of sand, the Ark searches still for the distant flutter of banners.

墨门的飞天之计，也同样如此。
百年无望，以千年记，方有一盼。
想通此事，他不过才入外门一年有余。
一切都是早就注定的安排，他一眼便看到了几十年后的自己。
钻研飞鸢机巧自然是有趣的，只是越是研习，越觉百年一眼可尽。
写几本书，制几样新式机巧。到头得一授名，再收三两个弟子。
那些弟子，或许将来也会走向他设想的路。
他总说滴水穿石、薤露有益。此理无错，却总觉自己少了些……冲动。
他能看到未来，但是他不知道要抵达这样的未来该如何坚持。
那每一滴落下水珠，其上的微茫，就合该是一样吗？
忽地，他觉得这世间的问题不该只有唯一解。
就算他们所有人奔赴的终点一致，这一路走来的方式，却可由自己决定。
古人云，读万卷书，行万里路。万卷书他读过了，万里路还在脚下。
现在，他要迈出去。
en:
To Brant, every riddle in this world had an answer. It was simply a matter of time.
Like water gnawing at stone, drop by drop, year after year, until a hole is finally pierced through. So it was for the Mohist quest for the heavens.
If a century yields no hope, then count by the millennium. Only then can a glimmer of hope be found.
With this realization, Brant had been in the outer sect just over a year.
It felt like a path already paved. In a single glance, he could see the man he would become decades from now.
Studying the intricate flying eagle mechanisms was undeniably fascinating. Yet the deeper he studied, the more those hundred years felt like a single, fleeting breath.
He'd write a few treatises and craft some new mechanisms. Eventually, he'd earn a name and take on a few disciples who might one day walk the path he had envisioned.
He often spoke of dripping water piercing stone, and the humble dew enriching the soil. The logic was sound, yet he felt a lack of... fire.
He could see the future, yet he didn't know how to hold on long enough to reach it.
Must every falling drop carry the exact same glint of hope?
Suddenly, it hit him: the riddles of this world need not have one single solution.
Though many strive toward the same destination, the paths they take are theirs alone to choose.
As the ancients said, "Read thousands of books and travel thousands of miles." He had read enough books. Now the journey lay before him.
Time to take the first step forward.

zh:
他是个短视眼。

打从他记事起，远山就是晕开的墨团，近树便是蓬松的绿云，人的面孔更是蒙着一道雾岚，五官都藏在了后面。
爹娘在他面前总乐呵呵的：“短视眼算个什么病呀，不打紧！”可那些翻卷了边的医书，一碗碗哄他喝下的药汁，甚至夜半时分偷偷烧化的符纸，他都隐约看得分明。
他并不觉得有什么，看不清，那就凑近些嘛。他看花，鼻尖凑到花蕊上，看书简，额头嵌进刻痕里。看人，则最想凑近人的眼睛，同样是在迷雾之下，有些人的眼灰蒙蒙，有些人却亮汪汪。
有一回，他凑到邻居家小妹妹脸跟前端详她的眼睛，把人家吓得大哭。第二天，邻居一家就搬走了，匆忙得近乎仓皇。他呆望着邻家空荡的院落，自责深深涌上来。从此便知要收敛许多，纵是再好看的人，也要忍住不轻易凑近。

可这方白太过例外。那天方白一出剑就打跑了所有人，艳阳天里逆着光，他觉得方白的眼睛比太阳还要亮。他多想把这双眼睛画下来，可惜出城的路太短，够说的话太少，他始终凑得不够近，没能看清那人眼底究竟盛着什么样的光彩。
不枉他扒车塞纸，竟真等来了方白的信。每回来信不过是些寻常田园事、琐碎江湖闻，可对不曾出过长安的他来说，便都是无限风光。
某日着了心魔一般，长安再也囿不住他。筷子当成毛笔，皂角看作干粮，一股脑塞入行囊，便跑出了家门。爹娘哭着追在后头，他只当二老要拦他，护着包裹不松手。爹娘扯着那包袱，泪汪汪将他胡乱塞错的物事拣出，换上妥帖的，又为他备上件最厚最暖的冬衣。
一路牵扯到城门口，他郑重而灿烂地回了头：“爹娘，我去吹吹外面的风！”
身后的叮咛渐渐被长风吹散，家越来越远，天地越来越近。

他走入了天地深处，却没再凑近过方白。唯一一次，却像是他臆想的。记忆总是这样，像浸了水的画。他只记得自己在模糊的天地间拼命地跑，怀中玉匣很硬很冷，风从耳畔掠过，方白背对着他，又似乎极其轻微地偏过头，回望了他一眼。那一眼，或许带着鼓励，或许带着诀别。
一瞬间，他的短视眼似乎痊愈了，世界前所未有地清明。他看清了草木的纹理，云朵的流动，人们面对他时的表情，一些人蹙起的眉头，另一些人眼底的慈悲。他甚至看清了许多年前邻居一家匆忙搬走的真相，看清了那日他莫名听到的金属碰撞声、呵斥声与呜咽声所意味着的画面。
他心神激荡，像一头迎风的狮子，为了拯救他曾因看不清而没能察觉的那一切，而奔跑着。

不记得风是何时停的。
终于抵达的长安，是一片死寂的废墟。宫阙楼宇，百司衙署，民间庐舍，成了承载不了任何故事、任何记忆的碎木头。水汽氤氲，远山默然，一根根焦黑梁木，横七竖八浮在浑浊的水面上，无声向下游漂去。
感到无措时，他试图回忆方白的脸。无论他怎么努力，脑海中只有一片比眼前更加彻底、更加绝望的模糊。
他好像，什么都看不清了。好像，从未有一刻看清过。
在一片空茫的死寂中，他缓缓地、缓缓地蹲下身，蜷缩起来。

他恨自己生来是个短视眼。
en:
For as long as he could remember, distant mountains were but smudges of ink, and nearby trees were nothing but soft, green clouds. Faces were veiled in a drifting mist, their features tucked away behind the haze.
His parents always smiled lightly, assuring him, "Being short-sighted isn't an illness; it's nothing to worry about." Yet behind their smiles, he saw the worn pages of medical books, tasted bitter medicines coaxed down in countless bowls, and even caught glimpses of talismans they burned in secret at midnight. They weren't as carefree as they pretended.
But he didn't fret. If the world was blurry, he'd simply lean in closer. When admiring flowers, he pressed his nose near their petals; in reading, his forehead was nearly pressed into the carved characters; and when looking at people, he longed most to peer into their eyes. Behind the same veil of mist, some eyes were dull as ash, while others shone like dewdrops.

Once, he leaned so close to the neighbor girl's face, studying her eyes with earnest curiosity, scaring her into a fit of tears. The next day, the family fled. He stood before their empty courtyard, a wave of guilt washing over him. From that day on, he learned restraint. No matter how captivating the face, he would hold himself back.

But Fang Bai... Fang Bai was an exception. That day, when he drew his sword and sent everyone fleeing, silhouetted against the day, his eyes seemed to burn brighter than the sun. How he longed to capture them in a painting, but the road out of the city was too short, their conversations too few, and he never got close enough to truly glimpse the light dwelling deep within those eyes.
All that effort, clinging to carriages just to slip him a note, hadn't been in vain. A letter finally arrived. Though filled with simple tales of rural life and trivial wandering adventures, to someone who had never left Chang'an, those words were nothing less than grand wonders. 
One day, as if possessed by a wanderlust demon, Chang'an could no longer hold him. He packed chopsticks, thinking they were brushes, and soap pods, thinking they were rations. His parents caught the bundle, tearfully unpacking the nonsense he'd stuffed inside. They replaced them with what he'd actually need, and tucked in the thickest, warmest winter coat they owned.
At the city gate, he looked back with bright confidence and said, "Mother, Father! I'm off to catch the wind!" Their voices faded on the growing breeze as home receded behind him, and the vast, open world beckoned, close, alive, and waiting.

He journeyed deep into the heart of the world, yet never drew close to Fang Bai again. The only time he did, it felt like a trick of the mind. Memory is always thus, a painting soaked in water, its ink bleeding away. What he truly remembered was racing through a hazy expanse, the jade box heavy and cold against his chest. The wind whispered past his ears, and while Fang Bai's back was to him, he seemed to tilt his head, just a fraction, and cast a glance back. Perhaps a look of encouragement, or a silent farewell.
In an instant, his sight was cured. The world turned sharp and clear as never before. He saw the delicate veins tracing through every leaf, the graceful flow of clouds across the sky, the subtleties in people's faces, some knitted in worry, others softened with kindness. Even the truth behind the neighbor family's abrupt departure, years past, unfolded before him: the clash of steel, the barks of command, and the muffled sobs... Now he finally saw what they meant.
His heart surged like a lion standing tall against the wind, propelled forward by an unyielding resolve to run, to fight, to save all those things he once failed to notice, blinded by his own limited sight.

He couldn't tell when the wind had finally fallen silent.
When he finally reached Chang'an, he found only a tomb of silence and ruin. Grand palaces, towering halls, government offices, humble dwellings, all reduced to splintered wood, too fragile to hold a single story, a single memory. The air hung thick with mist, the distant mountains kept their silence, and charred beams drifted aimlessly, tangling in the murky waters.

Lost and overwhelmed, he grasped desperately for an image of Fang Bai's face. There was only a blur, a darkness more absolute, more despairing than the ruin before him.
He loathed himself for being born with such short sight.

zh:
最恶浊的人学得所有，最璀璨的人却背乡远走。
后来的无数个深夜中，蛤蟆长老常常于梦中惊醒。而后恼恨于墨山道，这个他爱极又恨极的山门，这个徘徊又执着的山门。
空有天赋而无道心，彦希从不觉得自己配做墨家子弟，他只算一具空得技艺的躯壳。
幼时便被战火灼伤，他的心中只有深埋的恨意。那些高高在上的肉食之人，笑谈间可令千万人灰飞烟灭。相比于无数蝼蚁，战争中他们付出的代价太少太少，这便是这个天下的病灶。
只是这样一颗永远被复仇盈满的心，和墨山道太不相合。师兄师姐们的光芒时时刻刻温暖着他，又灼伤着他。彦希伪装着自己，他沉默寡言地仰望着，努力让自己能继续站在熠熠星辰之间。
但手中的机关术不会骗人。
他们手中会放飞飞鸢，而他的手下，则诞生各种淬毒、丑陋的机关虫——他只思考如何悄无声息地带走敌人的性命。被关进悬空屋，被禁绝学习师父的秘传机关术，他都不怨恨，他确实永远也无法变成师兄师姐们那样的人。
但忽然之间，光芒全部熄灭。他也没能抓住最后的机会，拦下他悄悄藏在心中最深处的那个人。
被师父从崖间悬空屋放出时，面对苍老了十岁的老人，他成了那个被山门彻底关死的人。
在生命的最后三年里，师父抓紧一切时间教授区彦希他的绝学，区彦希终于学会了他曾梦寐以求的机关术。
在最后一刻，老人弥留之时终于没有再谈机关术的事。他拉着区彦希的手，只重复着四个字：
“苦了你了……苦了你了……”
后来，区彦希戴上了四师姐给他做的蛤蟆面具，继任了阁主。他的头发早已花白，新的弟子们不知往事，都称呼他为蛤蟆长老。
那一年后，再没有人叫他小师弟了。
en:
The most depraved inherited all the knowledge, while the most radiant were driven into exile.
Blessed with genius but barren of "The Way," Yanxi never deemed himself worthy of the Mohist name. He was but a hollow vessel, overflowing with technique yet empty of spirit. Scarred by the flames of war in his youth, his heart harbored a hatred that ran bone-deep. Those high-born predators, feasting upon the world, could turn millions to ash with a casual jest. Compared to the nameless millions of ants, the cost they paid for their wars was infinitesimal. This was the true rot at the heart of the world.
But a heart so full of vengeance had no place in the Mohist Hill. The brilliance of his seniors was a constant presence. It warmed his soul even as it scorched his conscience. Yanxi wore a mask of silence, gazing upward from the depths, straining to keep his place among those shimmering stars.
But the craft within his hands could tell no lies. Where others' fingers loosed soaring kites, his brought forth venomous, grotesque mechanical vermin. He thought only of how to harvest lives in silence. When they confined him to the Aloft Abode and barred him from the master's deepest teachings, he didn't resent it. He knew he could never be like them.
But in an instant, all light was extinguished. He had failed his last chance to hold back the person whose name he dared not even whisper in the deepest corners of his heart.
Facing a master who seemed to have aged a decade in a single breath, he realized that he was the one now forever sealed within the sect.
During the final three years of the Master's life, Yanxi finally mastered the forbidden arts he had once dreamed of possessing.
At the end, as the old man lay dying, he no longer spoke of the craft. He gripped Yanxi's hand, repeating a single, broken phrase: "What a bitter road you've walked... what a bitter road..."
Later, Yanxi donned the toad mask crafted for him by his Fourth Sister and ascended as the new Master of the Hall. After that year, the words "Junior Brother" vanished from the world forever. Everyone called him the "Elder Toad."

……
大城丈五，为闺门，广四尺。为郭门，郭门在外，为衡，以两木当门，凿其木，维敷上堞。为斩县梁，令穿断城，以板桥邪穿外，以板次之，倚杀如城报。城内有傅壤，因以内壤为外。凿其间，深丈五尺，室以樵，可烧之以待适。

令耳属城，为再重楼，下凿城外堞，内深丈五，广丈二。楼若令耳，皆令有力者主敌，善射者主发，佐皆广矢。治裾诸，延堞，高六尺，部广四尺，皆为兵弩简格。转射机，机长六尺，貍一尺。两材合而为之辒，辒长二尺，中凿夫之为道臂，臂长至桓。二十步一，令善射之者佐，一人皆勿离。
……
en:
Mohist Hill Primer: Volume Two
...
The great wall stands fifteen feet high, featuring a secondary gate. It is four feet wide. An outer defensive gate is constructed. The outer gate serves as the vanguard, using two timbers to block the entrance, mortising the wood, and linking it to the battlements above. Construct a suspended drawbridge, allowing it to pierce through the severed wall, with wooden planks angling outward and subsequent planks following, leaning and reducing in scale like the wall itself. Pounded earth is used within the city, turning the inner earth into the outer defense. Dig a trench between them, fifteen feet deep, filling the chamber with firewood, ready to be ignited to await the enemy.
Construct projecting watchtowers attached to the wall, forming a double-tiered structure. Below, carve out outer battlements, fifteen feet deep inside and twelve feet wide. Both the towers and the projecting structures must be manned by those of great strength to repel the enemy, and by skilled archers to loose arrows; their assistants must all be supplied with broad-headed shafts. Establish elevated walkways extending along the battlements, six feet high, with a working width of four feet, all serving as storage racks for weapons and crossbows. Set up Swivel Crossbows; the mechanism is six feet long, buried one foot deep. Two timbers are joined to form the housing, which is two feet long. The center is mortised to serve as the track and arm, the arm reaching the pillars. Place one every twenty paces. Assign those skilled in archery to assist, and command that no man shall leave his post
. ...

zh:
大侠近来可好？
有一份心意想送与大侠。为免寄送延误，还请先行[<LINK id='link' color='#8c5823' url='https://research-game.163.com/htmls/46rzpk/paper.html?uid={uid}&role_id={pid}&server={hostnum}' is_underline='true'>点此留下信址</LINK>]。待我细细说来：
写这封信，是想给你报个喜。多亏你先前帮忙，我才有了支起摊子的本钱，在开封南郊的麦香集里寻了个落脚处。当初从家里出来时，哪敢想有今日……
爷爷常说，谢人不能只挂在嘴上。想来想去，我把近日攒下的钱寄回富平老家，用大侠的名义承包了五亩柿子地，托爷爷和乡亲们照看。爷爷说，要让你瞧瞧，特意让村里的老画师给画了下来，我都能想象后头红彤彤的模样了！
不过今年老家的天儿有些邪乎……又是旱又是涝的没断过，八成会影响收成……等到了做柿饼的时候，总要送你些尝尝，可能不多，但都是乡亲们的心意。不知大侠住在何处？一定包得仔仔细细的给你送去！
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/6937d9c2d01e3e9c8ead2dadl4zIiRj307' size='1810*2704' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
en:
Dear Wanderer,
How are you? I have a small token of my gratitude for you. To avoid any delay in its arrival, please press [<LINK id='link' color='#8c5823' url='https://research-game.163.com/htmls/46rzpk/paper.html?uid={uid}&role_id={pid}&server={hostnum}' is_underline='true'> to register your mailing address</LINK>] first. Allow me to explain:
I write with glad tidings. Thanks to your help, I've set up my stall at the Wheatwind Bazaar in Kaifeng Suburbs-South. When I left home, I never dreamed such a day…
Grandfather always said gratitude must be more than words. So I've sent my savings back to Fuping, my hometown, to lease five mu of persimmon groves in your name. Grandfather and the villagers tend them. He insisted on having the old painter paint them for you. I can already imagine the fiery red blaze!

zh:
舞狮兄弟是达安郑氏暴乱中的幸存者。
那年常喜十七岁，常乐六岁。两兄弟眼见宅中血流成河，而亲友尽数亡于流寇刀下。他们第一次知道，原来世道面前，善是如此虚妄与无力。后绝望的常喜抱着昏迷的弟弟仓皇出逃，却因力竭跌入河中，最后是鬼街六煞坤幺儿行经此地，一时心善救下了他们。次日醒来，常乐忘记了发生的一切。常喜便再不提及往事。他深知世道之恶，他无力抗衡；而血仇之深，眼下亦无力得报。于是他默默咽下一切，成为坤幺儿手下舞狮兄弟团的一员，借巡游之名为恩人搜集情报，并暗中等待一个合适的时机。
总有一日，他要向这世间的恶，讨回失去的一切。即便代价是，他也会沦为恶的一员。
en:
The Twin Lions are survivors of the Da'an Zheng Clan Rebellion. 
Back then, Chang Xi was seventeen years old, and Chang Le was just six. The two brothers watched helplessly as their home turned into a river of blood, their kin and friends all slaughtered by marauding bandits. It was then they first realized that in this chaotic world, kindness was but a hollow, powerless thing. In despair, Chang Xi fled with his unconscious younger brother in his arms, only to collapse from exhaustion and fall into a river. Kun the Youngest, one of the Six Fiends of Ghost Street, happened to be there and, moved by a rare moment of pity, saved their lives. When Chang Le awoke the next day, he remembered nothing of the horrors they had endured. Chang Xi never spoke of it again. He knew too well the cruelty of the world, a cruelty he could not hope to defy. And he knew the depth of his blood debt, a debt he had no power yet to repay. So, he swallowed his grief and rage, and became a member of the Twin Lions under Kun the Youngest, performing across the land under the guise of festival tours while secretly gathering intelligence for his benefactor. All the while, he waited. Biding his time for the right moment. 
He vowed that one day he would demand back all that was taken from him. Even if, in doing so, he had to become part of the evil he despised.

“景之大小，说在柂正、远近。”
以此度之，此倒景当于吾归山之日，当可三人共见。

吾出山游历前，已深觉己身微渺，飞天一途，茫茫不知何为。且留“水滴千日”之试予尔，亦为吾心所冀。待见山外之山，或有殊异。
今奔赴滹沱，忽有所感：何处需吾，便赴何处，薤露此益。
en:
Mid-afternoon. Water droplets trickle down from the eaves, each weighing one zhu, falling from a height of about nine feet.
By my calculations, it'll take twenty-four years for the dripping water to carve a hole three inches and seven fen deep.
And thereafter...
"The size of the shadow depends on the angle and distance."
Judging by this logic, the reflected scene should be visible to three people at once on the day I return to the mountain.

Before I left the mountain to travel the realm, I already felt how profoundly insignificant I was. The path to soaring into the sky is vast and uncertain, and I know not what to do. Leaving this "thousand-day water drop" experiment for you is also a token of my inner hopes. Perhaps after witnessing the mountains beyond our own, I will find a different perspective.

Now, as I rush toward the Hutuo River, a sudden realization strikes me: to go wherever I am needed, that is the true value of this fleeting life.

zh:
滹沱西南有一台地，层叠如阶，形如云梯，连绵成片，远望如一小丘，百姓沿梯耕耘，故名耘丘。
耘丘之中又有一营地，名镇戍仓，四方百姓耕种收获，皆聚集于此。平日安定时节，是为一方之粮仓；边关烽烟四起，可担输粟之枢纽。
常言道，耕乃战之基，粮为兵之脉。是以此地军民，虽分工各异，然上下同心，实为一体：日出各居其职，耕作运粮，井然有序；入夜则围篝火而坐，共话平生。
en:
To the southwest of the Hutuo River lies a stretch of high ground, rising layer upon layer like steps, shaped like a ladder to the clouds. It spreads out in terraces, and from afar looks almost like a low hill. The people farm and tend the land along these stepped slopes, and so the place came to be called Plowing Hill.
Within Plowing Hill, there is also a camp called Toilgrain Barn. The grain grown and harvested by the people of the surrounding region is gathered there. In peaceful times, it serves as the region's barn. When beacon fires flare along the frontier, it becomes a vital hub for transporting grain to the border.
As the saying goes, farming is the foundation of war, and grain is the lifeblood of an army. So although the soldiers and the local people each have their own duties, they work with one heart and are, in truth, one. By day, each goes about their own task, farming the land or hauling grain, all in good order. By night, they gather around the campfire and talk of their lives.

zh:
从前，范芗芗跟着爹娘逃荒，走到哪儿都饿。
那时候她还没长开，瘦得像豆芽菜。她娘把最后一把米熬成粥，那粥清得能照见人影。
她爹喝几口，便说饱了，剩下的一股脑推给她。可半夜里，她听见她爹的肚子咕噜噜响个没完。
后来她爹没撑住，倒在了路上。她娘哭了许久，眼瞎了，没几天人就走了。
范芗芗是被乐安浦的村民捡回来的，钱婆婆给她盛了碗白粥，上头还飘着油花。
她端着碗手抖，烫得直掉眼泪也舍不得撒手。那是她头一回觉得，吃饱饭是件能记一辈子的事。
如今范芗芗壮了，系着围裙在摊子后面忙活个不停。
她的摊子就支在村子里，一支便是二十年。
每天天不亮就起来炖鱼熬汤，做的饭油水特别足。
汤念念说她做饭像打仗，葱花一把一把地撒，油一勺一勺地挖，不把锅填满了不算完。
路过的流民隔老远就能闻到味儿，顺着香气摸过来，蹲在摊子边上看她忙活。
范芗芗也不问人从哪儿来，直接端上一碗热乎的。要是对方瘦得厉害，她还要多加几个馒头。
流民看着面前香喷喷的饭菜，不禁流下眼泪，感激的话不知该从何处说起。
“恁快吃，没啥大不了的！天塌了，也得先吃饱！”
en:
When she was a child, Fan Xiangxiang and her parents fled their home to escape the famine. Everywhere they went, hunger followed.
She was nothing but skin and bones back then. She still remembers her mother boiling their last handful of rice into a broth so watery she could see her reflection in it.
Her father took a few small sips, claimed he was full, and pushed the bowl to her. But that night, she lay awake in the dark, listening to his stomach rumble.
He didn't make it much farther before collapsing on the road. Her mother wept until she went blind, and passed away just a few days later.
A group of villagers from Tranquil Pier eventually found Xiangxiang and took her in. A woman named Granny Qian handed her a bowl of thick rice porridge, glistening with fat.
Xiangxiang's hands shook violently as she took it. The bowl was scalding hot, bringing tears to her eyes, but she refused to let go. That was the day she learned that the feeling of a full belly is something you never forget.
Today, Xiangxiang is a sturdy, healthy woman who spends her days bustling behind her village food stall, a stall she's run for twenty years now.
She's up before dawn every morning, stewing fish and simmering rich, heavy soups.
Tang Niannian likes to joke that Xiangxiang cooks like she's going to war: throwing in leeks by the fistful, ladling in generous scoops of oil, and refusing to stop until the pot is practically overflowing.
Wandering refugees can catch the savory scent from a mile away. They follow the aroma, eventually squatting down by her stall just to watch her work.
Xiangxiang never asks where they came from or what they've been through; she just hands them a piping-hot bowl of food. If they look dangerously thin, she makes sure to toss in a few extra steamed buns.
Staring down at the fragrant, heaping portions, the refugees often break down in tears, struggling to find the words to thank her.
"Eat up, it's nothing! Even if the sky is falling, you need to fill your belly first!"

zh:
李遇之梦到了一匹白马。
他时常做梦。梦到滂沱的雷雨，滔天的浊浪，师友们的哭嚎，和黄河水中飘散的白衣。
但这次不一样。他梦到了一匹白马从黄河之水中来。那浊水一分为二，白马就这么踏蹄而上。或许是长乐老的一句话，让他从回忆中打捞起了那个封存已久的夜晚。
青州将开文脉之学，依然名为文津馆。长乐老让他再收一个徒弟。这次，他们能保护好自己的徒弟了。
夜深露重，他的腿又开始隐隐作痛。纵是青溪圣手，也难以根除他的痼疾。那疼痛不断提醒他，他曾是多么失败的一位老师，护不住弟子的性命，也匡不正这天下。
而现在，他可以再试着重新做一次老师。

李遇之去集市上买了一匹白马，牵着它一步步走回山门。他半生官场浮沉，因腿脚不便时常骑马。但他从不骑白马，正如他这一生再也没有到过黄河边一样。
那位新弟子已经垂手立于树下，一双眼睛却止不住好奇地打量着周围。
“见过夫子。”稚童脆生生地行礼问好。李遇之恍惚了。已经很久没有听到这句话了。割据天下的枭雄称自己为先生，是为了求取诡谲的计策；金銮朝堂上的同僚称自己为相爷，是为了经营的交错人脉。他也习惯将自己藏在面具里，藏在官服下。可现在，孩子眼中尽是对自己的敬仰，和那纯粹的对学问的渴望。
“可会骑马？”李遇之笑了笑。“回夫子，不会……”弟子摇摇头。“还请、还请夫子教我！”弟子抬起头。“我听说夫子很厉害，不仅读的书多，还做过大官！夫子一定很会骑马吧！”李遇之点点头。“这匹马，就当做为师送你的见面礼。”
孩童忍不住地欢呼，道谢，央告着夫子将自己抱上马。李遇之将小弟子抱上马，替他调整马鞍，衔好马辔，检查脚蹬，又亲自上手摆正了小弟子的双腿。从始至终，他的手都紧紧抓着缰绳，未松一刻。

李遇之牵着一匹白马，带着自己的新弟子漫步在书院中。
“此处是膳厅，此处是洗砚池，那边是木铎钟……”李遇之紧紧攥着缰绳，好似怕丢掉了眼前的希望一般。“夫子，”小弟子怯生生地开口，“让我自己牵着缰绳吧。”
李遇之一口回绝。这匹马新买不久，还不知习性，万一发了狂伤到自己该如何？马背上的孩子瘪瘪嘴。“夫子一直这样牵着，我使不上力，学不会呀。”
是啊。李遇之看着自己的手。攥着缰绳的指节因用力而发白，磨得自己手上的疤生疼。但这样的疼却让他感觉到眼前的真实——自己又一次做了夫子，有了一位新的弟子。他太害怕了，怕自己的弟子又不见，自己又空欢喜一场。可迎上弟子的眼睛，李遇之又踟躇了。
若自己始终牵着缰绳，那他要怎么学会御骑之术？若自己始终不肯放手，那弟子又如何走自己的路呢。
“……夹紧，但要用腰发力，放松，”李遇之拍了拍马背，没抬起头， “别……别怕。”
“谢谢夫子！驾！”小弟子抓起缰绳，努力地挥动。
马儿似乎受了鼓舞，踏着步子往前奔。一开始，李遇之还能紧紧跟在后面，随后，马儿越来越快，李遇之便跟不上了。但这一次，他没有呼喊，只是那么一步，一步地跟在后面。
白色的马儿载着孩子的欢笑，哒哒地在书院的石径上跑了起来。马蹄声踏过缤纷的落英，仿佛回到了那些永远书不尽的春天。
en:
Li Yuzhi dreamed of a white horse.

He dreamed often: of pounding rain, of towering muddy waves, of the cries of teachers and friends, and of white robes drifting through the waters of the Yellow River. But this dream was different. He dreamed of a white horse emerging from the Yellow River, the turbid current parting as it rose step by step, hooves striking the water.

Perhaps it was Elder Changle's words that had stirred up that long-buried night from the depths of his memory. Qingzhou was about to reopen the school of the Inkbound Order, still under the name Inkbound Order. Elder Changle had asked him to take one more disciple.
This time, they would be able to protect their disciple.

Late that night, with dew heavy in the air, his leg began to ache again. Even the best healer at Silver Needle had never been able to cure that old injury. The pain was a constant reminder of what a failure he had once been as a teacher: unable to save his disciple's life, unable to set this world right. And now, he had one more chance to be a teacher.

Li Yuzhi went to the market and bought a white horse, then led it slowly back to the mountain gate. He had spent half his life drifting through officialdom, and because of his bad leg, he had often ridden on horseback. But he had never ridden a white horse, just as he had never returned to the Yellow River.

His new disciple was already waiting beneath a tree, hands lowered properly at his sides, though his eyes kept darting about with poorly hidden curiosity.
"Greetings, Master."
The child's voice was crisp and clear. Li Yuzhi faltered for a moment. It had been a very long time since he had heard those words.

The warlords who carved up the realm called him "Master" for his counsel. His colleagues in the gilded halls called him "Master" for the sake of power and favor. He too had grown used to hiding behind a mask, beneath the robes of office. But in this child's eyes, there was only admiration, and a pure, earnest desire to learn.

"Do you know how to ride?" Li Yuzhi asked with a smile.
The disciple shook his head. "No, Master... I don't."
Then he looked up again. "Please teach me! I've heard you're amazing. You've read so many books, and you were even a high official. You must be very good at riding too!"
Li Yuzhi nodded. "Then let this horse be my gift to you on the day we meet."
The child cheered, thanked him, and asked him to help him onto the horse. Li Yuzhi lifted the young disciple into the saddle, adjusted the tack, checked the stirrups, and even used his own hands to straighten the boy's legs. From beginning to end, he never loosened his grip on the reins for even a moment.

Li Yuzhi led the white horse and walked his new disciple slowly through the academy.

"This is the dining hall. This is the ink-washing pond. And over there is the Clarion Chime..."
He held the reins tightly, as though afraid of losing the hope before his eyes.
"Master," the young disciple said timidly, "let me hold the reins myself."
Li Yuzhi refused at once. The horse had only just been bought, and he still did not know its temperament. What if it bolted and threw him?
The child puffed out his cheeks. "If you keep holding the reins like that, I won't be using any strength at all. I'll never learn."

Yes. That was true.
Li Yuzhi lowered his gaze to his own hands. His knuckles had gone white around the reins, and the friction had rubbed the old scars on his palms raw. Yet the pain only made everything feel more real.

At last, he loosened his grip little by little and placed the reins in the child's hands.
The white horse gave a soft snort and pawed lightly at the ground, but it did not run.

The disciple held the reins carefully, as if cradling something precious, and looked back at him with delight shining in his eyes. "Master, look! I'm holding them!"
Li Yuzhi smiled. "Yes. Hold steady."
The child nodded earnestly and sat up even straighter in the saddle, trying his best to look the part.

In that moment, Li Yuzhi suddenly felt that perhaps all was not yet lost. Perhaps there was still time. Time to teach, time to protect, time to watch someone grow without seeing them taken by floodwaters, by war, or by the chaos of this broken age.

The mountain wind passed gently through the academy, stirring the leaves overhead. The young disciple sat on the white horse, bright with pride and joy, as though the whole world still lay open before him.
And Li Yuzhi, walking beside him with one hand resting lightly on the reins, felt for the first time in many years that the road ahead might still lead somewhere other than regret.

【地理·二】

【湖】

欹湖

望洞庭
